title: Slicing a list
objectives: Index a list from either end, including negative indices
Slice with a start, an end and a step, and predict the result
Tell a second name for a list from a copy of it

screens.title: Part of a list
screens.prose:
Six daily closes. The small numbers under the cells are the indices, counted from 0.

```python
closes = [101.20, 102.50, 99.80,
          100.40, 103.10, 104.00]
week = closes[1:4]
```
screens.question: Tap the closes that end up in `week`.

hints.text: A slice `[a:b]` starts at index `a`. Does it include index `b`?
The first cell is index 0, so index 1 is 102.50.
Indices 1, 2 and 3: the slice stops just before index 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at index 1 and stop before index 4.

byKey.end-in: You included index 4. A slice stops just before its end index.
byKey.from-one: You counted the first close as index 1. Python counts from 0, so `closes[1]` is 102.50.
byKey.c0: Index 0 is the first close, 101.20. The slice starts at index 1.
byKey.c4: Index 4 is the end of the slice, and a slice stops before its end.
byKey.c5: Index 5 is past the end of the slice `[1:4]`.
byKey.c1: You missed index 1, 102.50. A slice includes its start index.

explain.text: You kept indices 1, 2 and 3. A slice `[a:b]` starts at index `a` and stops before `b`, so it holds `b - a` items: here 3.

screens.prose: Python also counts from the end. `closes[-1]` is the last close. Slide to move the pointer, and read which cell each negative index names.

derive.ptr.label: closes[{{k}}]
derive.caption: closes[{{k}}] is the same cell as closes[{{6 + k}}]

screens.question: Which ordinary index names the same close as `closes[-2]`?

hints.text: Slide the pointer to −2 and read the small index under the cell.
`-1` is the last cell, index 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to −2 and read the index under the pointer.

byKey.sign: Index 2 counts from the front. A minus sign counts back from the end.
byKey.off: You counted one cell too far. `-1` is the last cell, index 5, so `-2` is index 4.

explain.text: At −2 the pointer sits on index 4, 103.10. A negative index `-k` means `len(closes) - k`: here `6 - 2 = 4`. So `closes[-1]` is always the latest close, however long the list grows.

screens.prose:
Taking a run of items this way is called **slicing**. Negative indices work in slices too, and a missing end means: run to the end.

```python
closes = [101.20, 102.50, 99.80,
          100.40, 103.10, 104.00]
print(closes[-3:])
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You stopped one cell early, as if the slice ended at `-1`. A missing end runs to the end of the list.
You took two cells. `-3` is the third from the end, index 3, and the slice starts there.
You read the list backwards. A slice keeps the original order unless you give it a negative step.

hints.text: Which ordinary index is `-3` in a list of 6?
Start at index 3 and run to the end: indices 3, 4 and 5.

feedback.correct: The last three closes, in their original order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn `-3` into an ordinary index, then run to the end.

explain.text: `-3` is index 3, and the missing end runs to the last cell. So `closes[-3:]` is always the latest three closes. Python prints 100.4, not 100.40: it drops trailing zeros.

screens.prose:
A slice can take a third number, the **step**: how far to jump each time. `closes[0:6:2]` takes indices 0, 2 and 4. A missing start means: from the beginning.

```python
odd_days = closes[1::2]
```
screens.question: Tap the closes in `odd_days`.

hints.text: The numbers are start, end and step. Here the end is missing.
Start at index 1, then jump 2 at a time.
Indices 1, 3 and 5; index 7 would be next, but the list ends at 5.

feedback.correct: From index 1 in steps of 2: indices 1, 3 and 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at index 1 and jump 2 each time.

byKey.from-zero: You started at index 0. The first number, 1, is the start.
byKey.two-on: You read `2` as the end. With two colons the numbers are start, end and step, and the end is left out.
byKey.c0: Index 0 comes before the start, index 1.
byKey.c2: Index 2 is skipped: from index 1, a step of 2 lands on 3.
byKey.c4: Index 4 is skipped: the steps land on 1, 3 and 5.

explain.text: From index 1 the step of 2 lands on 1, 3 and 5, and the missing end lets it run to the last cell. Index 7 would be next, but there is none.

screens.title: The latest closes
screens.prose: A backtest often needs the latest `n` closes. Assume `0 <= n <= len(prices)`. Hidden tests try every allowed `n`, including the smallest.
screens.question: Write `last_n(prices, n)` that returns the last `n` prices as a list.

widget.starter:
def last_n(prices, n):
    pass  # replace this line
widget.solution:
def last_n(prices, n):
    return prices[len(prices) - n:]
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests that call your function. Each answer must equal the expected value exactly (`==`).

hints.text: Where does the run of the last `n` start, counted from the front?
Run test 4 in your head. What is `-0`?
`return prices[len(prices) - n:]` starts `n` cells before the end, and works when `n` is 0.

feedback.correct: `len(prices) - n` marks where the last `n` begin, even when `n` is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test and work its slice out by hand.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 asks for the last 0 prices and expects `[]`. If you got the whole list, you wrote `prices[-n:]`: with `n` = 0 that is `prices[0:]`, because −0 is 0.

explain.text:
`len(prices) - n` is the index where the last `n` begin. The tempting `prices[-n:]` breaks at `n = 0`, because `-0` is just 0 and the slice takes everything.

```python
prices[-n:]              # n = 0 gives the whole list
prices[len(prices) - n:] # n = 0 gives []
```

screens.question: Write `fridays(closes)` that returns the Friday closes, using one slice.

widget.starter:

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests that call your function. Each answer must equal the expected value exactly (`==`).

hints.text: You need a start, no end, and a step.
The first Friday is index 4, and Fridays are 5 apart.
`return closes[4::5]`

feedback.correct: Start at 4, run to the end, step 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your slice's start and step with the highlighted cells.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[103.1, 105.2]`. If you got `[101.2, 104.0]`, your slice started at 0; start at index 4. If you got only one value, check that the end is left out.

explain.text: `closes[4::5]` starts at the first Friday and jumps a week each time. Test 2 is an edge case: with only three closes there is no Friday, and the slice is empty rather than an error.

screens.prose:
Before adding today's close, you keep a backup of the list in `b`.

```python
a = [101.20, 102.50, 99.80]
b = a
a.append(100.40)
print(len(b))
```
Each name is a card; each box is a list object in memory.
screens.question: What does the last line print?

options.why: You treated `b = a` as a copy. It puts a second name on the same list, so the append shows through both.
`len` counts the items. It returns a number, not the list.

options.text: An error: `b` has no list of its own
options.why: `b` is a valid name for the same list, so `len(b)` works.

hints.text: Does `b = a` build a new list, or name an existing one?
Only one line in the program builds a list.
`b = a` makes `b` a second name for the one list. After the append that list has 4 closes.

feedback.correct: One list, two names: the append shows through `b`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many lists the program builds.

byKey.copy: You treated `b = a` as a copy. It puts a second name on the same list, so the append shows through both.

explain.text: `b = a` stuck a second name on the same list. `append` changed that one list, so both names see four closes. Assignment never copies a list.

screens.prose:
Every slice builds a new list, so `a[:]`, the slice with no start and no end, is a full copy.

```python
a = [101.20, 102.50]
b = a
c = a[:]
```
screens.question: Drag each name onto the list it labels.

hints.text: Which lines build a list, and which only add a name?
`c = a[:]` slices, and a slice is always a new list.
`a` and `b` go on the line 1 list; `c` goes on the line 3 list.

feedback.correct: `b` shares the original; `c` has its own copy.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Assignment adds a name; slicing builds a list.

byKey.a: `a` names the list built on line 1.
byKey.b: `b = a` copies the name, not the list, so `b` belongs on the line 1 list.
byKey.c: `a[:]` is a slice, and every slice builds a new list. `c` labels that new list.

explain.text: `b = a` added a name; `a[:]` built a new list with the same values. Now `a.append(...)` changes what `b` sees, but never `c`.

screens.title: Leave the caller's list alone
screens.prose: A function that adds a close should not change the list it was given: someone else may hold a name for it. Build a new list instead.
screens.question: Write `with_close(closes, price)` that returns a new list: `closes` with `price` on the end. Leave `closes` unchanged.

widget.starter:
def with_close(closes, price):
    pass  # replace this line
widget.solution:
def with_close(closes, price):
    new = closes[:]
    new.append(price)
    return new
widget.how: Check runs 4 hidden tests that call your function. Each answer must equal the expected value exactly (`==`).

hints.text: If you `append` to `closes` itself, the caller's list grows.
Copy first with a slice, then append to the copy.
`new = closes[:]`, then `new.append(price)`, then `return new`.

feedback.correct: The copy grew; the caller's list did not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 returns your result and the original list side by side. If the original grew too, you appended to `closes` itself; copy it with `closes[:]` first.

explain.text:
`closes[:]` built a new list, and only that list grew. Test 2 shows the original afterwards: still two closes.

```python
closes.append(price)   # changes the caller's list
new = closes[:]        # a copy you are free to change
```

screens.prose: Every slice you took followed one rule: start at $i$, jump by $k$, stop before $j$. $$\texttt{a[i:j:k]} = [\,a_i,\ a_{i+k},\ a_{i+2k},\ \dots\,]$$ With a step of 1 it holds $j - i$ items. Every slice is a new list.
screens.question: A list holds 10 closes. How many items are in `closes[2:7]`?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the start from the end.

byKey.both: You counted index 7 too. The slice stops before its end.
byKey.end: That is the end index, not the count. Subtract the start: 7 − 2.

explain.text: The slice takes indices 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, stopping before 7. That is $7 - 2 = 5$ items, the same $j - i$ count as `closes[1:4]` gave 3 on the first screen.

screens.title: A moving average
screens.prose: Traders watch the 5-day average: the mean of the latest five closes. A close above it is read as strength. Assume `1 <= n <= len(closes)`.
screens.question: Write `sma(closes, n)` that returns the mean of the last `n` closes.

widget.starter:
def sma(closes, n):
    pass  # replace this line
widget.solution:
def sma(closes, n):
    return sum(closes[-n:]) / n
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests that call your function. A number is accepted when it is within `math.isclose` of the expected value.

hints.text: Take the last `n` closes with a slice, then average them.
`sum(xs)` adds a list of numbers.
`return sum(closes[-n:]) / n`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which closes your slice took in test 1.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects 103.48, the mean of the last five. If you got 101.40, your slice took the first five instead.

explain.text: `closes[-n:]` takes the last `n` closes, `sum` adds them and dividing by `n` gives the mean: £517.40 / 5 = £103.48. Since `n` is at least 1, the `-0` edge case cannot bite here.

ideas: `a[i:j:k]` starts at index `i`, jumps by `k`, and stops before `j`. A missing part means: from the start, to the end, or a step of 1.
A negative index counts from the end: `a[-k]` is `a[len(a) - k]`.
`b = a` adds a second name for one list. A slice such as `a[:]` builds a new list.

formula.name: Slice
formula.note: With step 1 it holds $j - i$ items.

summary.trap: `b = a` does not copy: change the list through `a` and `b` sees it. Copy with `a[:]`.

options.why: You ignored the step. A step of −1 walks backwards from the end.
That is `closes[-1:]`. Here the `-1` is the step, after two colons.

options.text: An error: a step cannot be negative
options.why: A negative step is allowed. It walks from the end towards the start.

feedback.correct: A step of −1 walks the list backwards.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With two colons, the third number is the step.

explain.text: With no start or end, a step of −1 runs from the last item back to the first. `closes[::-1]` is a reversed copy; `closes` itself is unchanged.

options.why: You treated the slice like an index. `closes[10]` fails, but a slice past the end just stops at the end.
Python never pads a slice. It returns only the items that exist.
Indices 2 and 3 exist, so the slice keeps them.

feedback.correct: A slice past the end stops at the end.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which of indices 2 to 9 exist?

explain.text: Indices 2 and 3 exist; 4 to 9 do not, and a slice quietly stops at the end. An index past the end, like `closes[10]`, raises `IndexError` instead.

quiz.prose:
```python
a = [1.5, 2.5]
b = a[:]
c = a
a.append(3.5)
print(len(b), len(c))
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You treated the slice as a second name. `a[:]` built a new list, so `b` kept 2 items.
You treated `c = a` as a copy. `c` is another name for `a`'s list, so it sees the append.
That swaps the two. The slice `b` is the copy; `c` shares the list.

feedback.correct: `b` is a copy and kept 2; `c` shares the list and sees 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which line built a new list?

explain.text: `b = a[:]` built a copy before the append, so it still has 2 items. `c = a` is a second name for the same list, which now has 3.

quiz.prose: `closes` holds 20 daily closes, at indices 0 to 19.
quiz.question: How many items are in `closes[1:20:3]`?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the indices: start at 1 and add 3 while below 20.

byKey.dropped-last: You stopped at 16. Index 19 is still below the end, 20, so it counts.
byKey.divided: That is the span from 1 to 20. The step of 3 takes every third index.

explain.text: From 1, steps of 3 give 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 and 19. The next, 22, is past the end. That is 7 items.
